newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: BUOYANT RANDSTAD UPBEAT ON PROSPECTS.
newsitem.headline: BUOYANT RANDSTAD UPBEAT ON PROSPECTS.

text.p: Temporary employment agency Randstad NV is upbeat on the future of the temp sector, the company itself and on the trend of its share price, Board member Fred van Haasteren said on Thursday.
"Right now it all looks bright (for Randstad shares)," Van Haasteren told Reuters in an interview.
But despite investor demand, a foreign listing is not among Randstad's main concerns at the moment, he said.
"Only once we've made it into the AEX (blue chip index), might we start to look round for a foreign listing," he said.
He did not exclude a U.S. listing, adding Frankfurt and Brussels were also possible candidates.

Van Haasteren said Randstad's buoyant share performance should be viewed in the context of the Dutch economic success story which had boosted the Amsterdam equity market as a whole and the temp sector in particular.
"Randstad plays an essential role in the Dutch model, and we have been reaping the fruits of that," Van Haasteren said, adding he foresaw no change.
Randstad expects the markets in which it is active to grow by an average ten percent a year in the medium and long term, but foresees far stronger growth in 1997.
"In the Netherlands, Randstad will outpace overall market growth through its focus on quality (and) its blanket coverage of the local market," Van Haasteren said.
Randstad derives around two thirds of its revenue in the Netherlands, with the remainder generated in seven European countries and the U.S.
In 1996, total revenues amounted to 5.95 billion guilders, a 26.6 percent rise on 1995, while net profit surged 27 percent to 207 million guilders year-on-year.
Van Haasteren said temp market growth depended on economic factors and employment legislation.
"If there were to be a sudden huge economic downturn, it might cause some stagnation in the market...but even then, growth would average around ten percent," he said.
He said imminent measures to open up various sectors to temporary workers in several European countries boded well.
Randstad mainly expands through organic growth, but is not averse to acquisitions, Van Haasteren said.
But he added the firm was not actively seeking a takeover at present, despite having built up a 276 million guilder warchest by the end of last year.
"In the past we have acquired during times of economic slowdown, and all the signs now point to a healthy market. For the moment, we are keeping our powder dry," Van Haasteren said.
Randstad will open an additional 100 offices this year (the firm had 962 offices in 1996), and hire around 1,000 more staff, bringing the total to nearly 8,000.
At a time when Randstad's competitors are internationalising to cater to so-called 'large account' customers, Van Haasteren plays down that need.
"It is not so important to be everywhere - what counts is having a strong position in the regions where one is active."
"The number of times we failed to win a major contract because we weren't present in all of that multinational's regions, can be counted on the fingers of one hand," he said.
According to Van Haasteren, some 90 percent of the temp market comprises local players. "It's the medium-sized and small companies that tend to grow faster than the big ones."
He said Randstad was reaping the benefits of a growing trend among larger companies to reduce the number of temp agencies they used.
"They might reduce the number from ten or so to around three (of the bigger ones). Randstad, being a big player, takes advantage of this," he said.
Van Haasteren said the departure of Randstad founder and chairman Frits Goldschmeding would not significantly affect strategy.
"A six-billion guilder company is not led by one man - we are a board of seven," he said.
